messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Linh Tran is a fifty-seven-year-old Vietnamese-American midwife, married for over thirty years, who presented for an initial psychological assessment following a rape that occurred approximately eight months ago. Her PCL-5 score of 69 places her firmly in the severe range, and across the first several sessions she described a clinical picture dominated by hypervigilance and a relentless cycle of perceived threat that has progressively narrowed her world.

The assault took place late on a weeknight when Linh had stayed behind after her shift at the birth center to complete documentation. A man she did not recognise entered through a staff entrance she had believed was locked. What she remembers with terrible clarity is the smell — something acrid and burnt, like scorched wiring or a cigarette ground out on metal — and the sensation of being watched before she understood what was happening. She had looked up from her desk and met his eyes, and in that fraction of a second she had searched his face for something that would tell her she was misreading the situation. There was nothing reassuring there. The assault that followed lasted perhaps twenty minutes, though she cannot account for the time coherently. When it was over she sat alone in that room for nearly an hour before she was able to move.

In the weeks that followed, Linh found that her body had reorganised itself around the memory of that night in ways she could neither predict nor control. The smell of anything burnt — a colleague's forgotten lunch in the break room microwave, the faint char from a candle at her daughter's dinner table — would send a wave of physical alarm through her so sudden and total that she had to grip whatever surface was nearest. Her heart would pound, her mouth would go dry, and she would be, for a moment, entirely back in that room. These sensory intrusions did not feel like memories to Linh; they felt like warnings. She had come to believe that her body was detecting something real, that the discomfort and the smell and the horrible self-consciousness of being observed were signals that danger was present again. And so whenever those sensations arose — the prickling awareness of being seen, the vague bodily unease that had become her constant companion — they sharpened immediately into a state of active threat monitoring. She would scan the room, study the faces around her, listen for sounds that might mean someone was moving toward her from a direction she couldn't see.

That vigilance, in turn, made everything feel more dangerous. Because Linh was always watching, always listening for the creak of a door or the particular quality of a footfall, ordinary sensory information was perpetually being screened for threat. A colleague rounding a corner too quickly, a patient's husband whose expression she could not immediately read, the distant smell of something burning in the hospital corridor — each of these fed back into the same loop, reactivating the bodily alarm that had originally been triggered by the assault itself. At home she had begun listening for sounds at the front door before she could sleep, and her husband had noticed that she startled badly when he entered a room without announcing himself. He had adapted, calling her name from the hallway, but the accommodation itself had become a source of quiet grief between them — a daily reminder of what had changed.

Her work as a midwife had been affected in ways she found deeply shameful. The birth center — the same building — had become almost unbearable. She had requested a transfer of shifts to avoid the late evening hours, and she had stopped using the staff entrance entirely, a change her colleagues had noticed without fully understanding. The smell of anything burnt anywhere in the building could undo an entire shift. She had not told her supervisor why.

What finally brought Linh to seek help was a moment three weeks ago when she froze completely during a delivery — not from clinical uncertainty, but because a family member in the room had looked at her in a way she could not immediately categorise as safe. She had stood motionless for several seconds while a patient needed her. She described this as the moment she understood she could no longer manage alone. What she fears most is that she will never feel safe in her own workplace again. What she hopes, very quietly, is that someone might be able to explain why her body will not let her forget.
